[2610.02905#1] **Abstract**
Classical reactive molecular dynamics of boron- and lithium-conditioned tungsten surfaces show that the order in which boron and oxygen are introduced - not the boron inventory - controls surface chemistry. On a thin engineered tungsten oxide, boron captures 81% of oxygen and consumes the oxide; on an engineered ~2 nm mixed WO3/WO2 film, boron captures only 20% and leaves 52% of reaction-zone tungsten in WO3-like coordination; and in a co-deposited W-B substrate later exposed to oxygen, boron captures only 28% despite a tenfold larger inventory. Adding lithium leaves the oxide-first cases unchanged but transforms the co-deposited case, where lithium becomes the dominant oxygen captor (58%) and a lithium-borate-glass-like network form. We outline the expected, divergent responses of the boron-only and boron-plus-lithium materials to deuterium irradiation.

[2610.02905#1] **Abstract**
Classical reactive molecular dynamics of boron- and lithium-conditioned tungsten surfaces show that the order in which boron and oxygen are introduced - not the boron inventory - controls surface chemistry. On a thin engineered tungsten oxide, boron captures 81% of oxygen and consumes the oxide; on an engineered ~2 nm mixed WO3/WO2 film, boron captures only 20% and leaves 52% of reaction-zone tungsten in WO3-like coordination; and in a co-deposited W-B substrate later exposed to oxygen, boron captures only 28% despite a tenfold larger inventory. Adding lithium leaves the oxide-first cases unchanged but transforms the co-deposited case, where lithium becomes the dominant oxygen captor (58%) and a lithium-borate-glass-like network form. We outline the expected, divergent responses of the boron-only and boron-plus-lithium materials to deuterium irradiation.

Boronization and lithiation are routinely used to condition the plasma-facing components (PFCs) of magneticconfinement fusion devices, suppressing intrinsic impurities, gettering oxygen and controlling fuel recycling [16]. Mikhail Roiz<sup>∗1,2</sup> , Rashid Valiev<sup>†3</sup> , Jan-Lucas Eickmann<sup>1,2</sup> , Theo Kurten<sup>3</sup> , Benjamin Brecht<sup>1,2</sup> , Michael Stefszky<sup>1,2</sup> , and Christine Silberhorn<sup>1,2</sup> > 1Paderborn University, Integrated Quantum Optics, Institute for Photonic Quantum Systems (PhoQS), Warburger Str. 100, 33098 Paderborn, Germany > 2Paderborn University, Institute for Photonic Quantum Systems (PhoQS), Warburger Str. 100, 33098, Paderborn, Germany > 3Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, P.O. Virtanens plats 1), FIN-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland October 5, 2026 #### **Abstract** Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) has provided strong evidence of quantum advantage, motivating the search for real-world applications. Such applications rely on mapping physical problems to the native GBS output: photon-number patterns sampled from a highly non-trivial probability distribution. Here we derive a GBS-compatible mapping for the rate constant _k_ IC of internal conversion (IC), incorporating two important physical effects – Duschinsky rotations and Herzberg– Teller contribution. We validate this framework using sampling _simulations_ of dibenzoterrylene, reproducing reported values of _k_ IC. Beyond _k_ IC reconstruction, we show that the photon-number patterns of GBS encode the vibrational mode combinations responsible for the IC process, which we refer to as non-radiative pathways. This pathway-resolved data can then be grouped in different ways to extract

[2610.03271#1] Pathway-resolved analysis of internal conversion enabled by Gaussian boson sampling
multiple physically motivated observables. In particular, it enables _k_ IC analysis at several levels, from individual modes and mode family contributions to recurring vibrational configurations shared by multiple pathways. We find that Duschinsky rotations increase the fraction of _k_ IC associated with correlated vibrational pathways from 46% to 86%, and identify the mode combinations with the largest rate contributions. These pathway-resolved insights can guide targeted molecular modifications, including selective deuteration and bond substitution, to control non-radiative decay. Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) [1,2] has been established as a scalable, non-universal photonic quantum computing platform for demonstrating quantum advantage – a scenario in which a quantum computing device outperforms all possible classical algorithms for a given task [3–9]. An important next step is therefore to extend existing demonstrations of quantum advantage towards practically relevant tasks. This has motivated an active search for applications that naturally map onto the GBS platform [10–19]. Such mappings rely on the native output of GBS, which is the sampling of photon-number patterns from a highly non-trivial probability distribution [1, 2]. One of the first applications that aimed to exploit this property was the simulation of molecular vibronic spectra [10, 11]. In this application, each photon-number pattern can

[2610.03271#2] Pathway-resolved analysis of internal conversion enabled by Gaussian boson sampling
be mapped to a specific vibronic transition, described by a distinct > ∗Corresponding author, mikhail.roiz@uni-paderborn.de > †Corresponding author, rashid.valiev@helsinki.fi 1 combination of vibrational quanta among molecular modes. The strength of each specific transition is given by a Franck–Condon factor (FCF), which under the GBS mapping can be estimated from the probability of the corresponding photon-number pattern [10,11]. The complete set of these transitions defines a multi-dimensional observable – the _mode-resolved vibronic spectrum_ – which contains the exact combinations of vibrational quanta among the modes. Reconstructing the full mode-resolved spectrum with GBS, however, requires exponentially many samples as molecular size grows [20, 21]. This necessitates _grouping_ sampled photon patterns into lower-dimensional quantities defined by the target physical observable [20, 21]. In spectroscopy, this observable is usually the spectral envelope (or Franck-Condon profile) [10,20], obtained by grouping individual vibronic transitions into finite-width energy bins, effectively erasing information about combinations of vibrational quanta among modes [20]. While this grouping overcomes the issue of needing exponentially many samples, the reduced task no longer exploits the complete information contained in photon-number patterns – in fact, it can be calculated efficiently using classical Fouriertransform methods [20–24]. Utilizing the ground-state density as the input to the ML model is motivated by the Hohenberg-Kohn and Runge-Gross theorems, and the fact that the groundstate density encodes information about bonding, charge localisation, and electronic delocalisation. The question we test is whether the benefits of using the density outweigh the (notprohibitive) penalty of requiring an additional singlepoint DFT calculation for the density. [2610.03462#38] **IV. CONCLUSIONS**
The recommended workflow for calculating instanton rate constants for bridge-mediated processes is as follows: first, the reactant–product MECP is located and _V_ R, _V_ P and _V_ B are calculated at this point. The relevant regime is identified based on whether the energy of _V_ B is above or below _V_ R and _V_ P, and the appropriate instanton pathway is optimized. Note that as the instanton hopping points are not necessarily at the MECP, the potentials along the instanton pathway should be double-checked to ensure that the correct regime was chosen. In a borderline case, the uniform approximation must be used. This is especially important in the high-bridge regime, where the leading-order instanton rate can diverge. However, as the maximum extra work required to evaluate the uniform correction is one additional gradient and Hessian calculation on the bridge at the hopping points, it is recommended to be used in general. With the extension to the high-bridge regime, we significantly expand the applicability of bridge-mediated instanton theory. This construction is effective for many vertical excitations, but does not directly provide a state-specific perturbation theory especially for a reference with optimized orbitals. Such references are of interest because orbital relaxation can be essential when the electronic structure changes substantially upon excitation, including charge-transfer states<sup>12</sup> . Several CIS-based approaches incorporate orbital relaxation at different levels, including variationally orbital-adapted CIS<sup>13</sup> , excited-state mean-field (ESMF) theory<sup>14–16</sup> , double CIS (DCIS)<sup>17</sup> , and state-averaged CIS (SACIS)<sup>18,19</sup> . SACIS also enables the description of conical intersections without specifying an active space. These approaches nevertheless require additional dynamical correlation for quantitative excitation energies. This motivates a perturbative correction defined in terms of the excited-state reference itself. Excited-state Møller–Plesset perturbation theory (ESMP2) follows this strategy by correlating an ESMF reference<sup>14,20</sup> . Its original _O_ ( _N_<sup>7</sup> ) cost was reduced to _O_ ( _N_<sup>5</sup> ) through a modified zeroth-order Hamiltonian and an approximation to the triples sector based on natural transition orbitals (NTOs). [2610.03613#2] I. INTRODUCTION
When solids are suspended in an electrolyte solution of concentration n∞, they typically assume a certain surface charge density σ and a surface potential Φs that are linked to each other. For non-conducting materials, σ remains constant and is independent of salt concentration. Importantly, many surface phenomena are driven by Φs and not, as one might initially think, by surface charge density, and do not depend on the potential profile near the surface. The best-known examples include the limiting value of the ionic density at the boundary [1] and electrokinetic phenomena [2]. Consequently, once the relation between σ and Φs is known, the limiting osmotic pressure or macroscopic electrokinetic response can be found without analyzing the full potential profile in the solution. A closed-form analytical relationship between σ and Φs can be obtained by the first integration of the secondorder Poisson–Boltzmann equation. However, due to its non-linearity, exact solutions exist only for a limited number of simple configurations. For a planar wall, the exact solution is given by the Grahame equation, also known as the contact theorem [1, 3, 4]. [2610.04107#2] **I. INTRODUCTION**
The inherent complexity of wave-function-based quantum chemical methods such as coupled cluster (CC) theory<sup>1–7</sup> is a challenge to the development of highly optimized production-level software implementations. Even at moderate levels of electron correlation (up to triple excitations), the CC amplitude equations alone involve dozens of tensor contractions,<sup>8</sup> and careful validation and testing at each stage of development is essential for robust, trustworthy code. In addition, while optimized code is naturally highly sophisticated, it is typically accessible only to experts and thus presents a large learning curve for students and other newcomers to the field. Simpler, well-documented reference codes can be invaluable for exploratory and/or educational purposes. [2610.04107#49] **XI. CONCLUSIONS AND PROSPECTUS**
PyCC is a Python-based code whose purpose is fourfold: (1) to deliver a clear reference implementation of a range of quantum chemical wave-function-based methods; (2) to provide a validation suite for the development of largescale production-level implementations in packages such as Psi4; (3) rapid prototyping of new ideas, such as localCC based on PNO++ and CPNO++ perturbation-aware correlation spaces or RT-CC3; and (4) to contribute to the education of neophytes in the basic algorithms of quantum chemical models. The code is fully open source, meaning that its entire development history (as well as current efforts) are publicly exposed at its GitHub repository.<sup>64</sup> PyCC is **not** intended to provide a productionlevel, optimized computational infrastructure for large molecules. While its algorithms do not fully duplicate advanced infrastructure, they do include important efficiency measures such as disk-based storage of quantities that are expensive to compute and store in core memory, as well as AO-based approaches in derivative calculations that minimize the costly AO-to-MO transformation of perturbation-dependent quantities. Thus, PyCC reaches beyond “toy” problems into realistic test cases that can serve to stress emerging models. For example, our recent efforts include simulation of the VCD spectrum of 3-chloro-1-butyne at the CISD/cc-pVTZ level of theory

PyCC has proven its worth for rapid-prototyping and testing of new methods, especially in the area of localcorrelation/reduced-scaling CC methods.<sup>41–43</sup> The package has two distinct local-CC execution modes: a “simulation” approach that uses the canonical-MO code to filter non-local contributions iteration-by-iteration and a genuine pairwise (localized occupied-MO) algorithm that more directly mimics a fully optimized code. The PyCC local-CC code provides four potential virtualorbital spaces: (1) PAOs<sup>35–37</sup> , the AO basis with the localized occupied MO contributions projected out — one overall virtual space with subspaces selected on a per-occupied-MO-pair basis; (2) PNOs,<sup>38</sup> pair natural virtual orbitals constructed separately for each localized occupied-MO pair; and (3) PNO++/CPNO++,<sup>39–41</sup> PNOs replaced or augmented, respectively, by contributions from the perturbation-dependent pair densities. These spaces are selected and deployed through a Local class which handles the construction of the localized virtual spaces, as well as the relevant transformation matrices. The occupied MOs are localized by the base Wavefunction class using either the Pipek-Mezey<sup>61</sup> or Foster-Boys<sup>62</sup> approaches, and the local-CC codes are limited to spatial MOs only at present. The local-simulation code within the Local class 11 uses an approach originally described by Hampel and Werner<sup>36</sup> and works through the canonical-MO CC codes in PyCC.

[2610.04107#32] **C. Property Facade**
In order to simplify the user interface, standard properties may be requested through a general set of functions, including dipole, gradient, polarizability, optical_rotation, hessian, apt, and aat. Each function requires a {MP/CI/CC}deriv object and not just a {MP/CI/CC}wfn object for two reasons. The first is to avoid cases in which, for example, the user re-computes the wave function amplitudes using different convergence criteria after the creation of {MP/CI/CC}deriv. The latter creates a snapshot of the converged wave function (including Λ<sup>ˆ</sup> in the case of CCderiv), thus protecting the property calculations from changes in the state of the original wave function parameters that would cause a mismatch with densities and other components computed from the previous set of converged parameters. The second reason for requiring a {MP/CI/CC}deriv object for the property interface is to ensure consistent use of the DerivStore disk-caching system. Each of the perturbed tensors in the DerivStore is identified by the CorrelatedDerivs object that owns it. This prevents two or more CorrelatedDerivs objects ( _e.g._ an MPderiv and a CCderiv existing simultaneously from accidentally accessing the same DerivStore tensors). Each property function returns a PropertyComponents object that includes the nuclear (if any), Hartree-Fock 9 reference, and correlation contributions

[2610.04107#11] **A. The Wavefunction Base Class**
The Wavefunction class holds a set of common components used by every quantum chemical method in PyCC. The SCF reference wave function, ref, is computed by the Psi4 package<sup>51</sup> and provided to the constructor by the user. The ref provides Wavefunction with the molecular orbital (MO) coefficients, the SCF energy, nuclear repulsion energy, frozen-core data, orbital symmetries, and other attributes. While PyCC does not make use of point-group symmetry in its calculations, it accepts MOs that are either symmetrized or unsymmetrized. In addition, the MO basis is automatically resolved from the reference by default either as ’spatial’ for closedshell RHF references or ’spinorbital’ for any reference, and these choices also yield key information about the number of occupied/virtual orbitals and NumPy slices, spin-to-spatial-MO mappings, etc. Furthermore, the Wavefunction builds and maintains several key helper classes, as depicted in Fig. 1.

However, the symmetric ap- proach is still somewhat less expensive than the asymmetric route because the expressions for the perturbed ˆΛ amplitudes involve significantly more tensor contractions, resulting in a larger prefactor. Both implementations yield identical results, which provides a validation check between the two distinct formulations. We test the AutoSella optimizers along two generalization axes. _Molecules:_ four held-out datasets comprising 500 PubChem molecules selected to be dissimilar from the training and validation sets, 673 dipeptides, 475 amino acid–ligand pairs, and 100 Solvated PubChem systems. Neither gate inspects the geometry itself, so we additionally compare the optimized conformations with the ones from Sella, by heavy-atom RMSD and by vibrational analysis, in Appendix E. Figure 2 illustrates the autoresearch progress and how the gates reject candidates.

[2610.06577#2] ABSTRACT
Geometry optimization is a major cost in many quantum-chemical workflows: each optimization step requires one force evaluation, and at the density-functional level that evaluation dominates the wall time. Research in this area has produced a broad range of optimization methods, and we ask whether a language model can improve on the best of them through autoresearch. An agent rewrites the optimizer itself to minimize force-call counts, restrained by two admission gates that reject premature stopping and improvements that do not generalize to unseen molecules. Starting from Sella, the fastest open-source optimizer available, the search produces AutoSella, a family of two optimizers. Both of them deliver consistent force-call reductions relative to Sella across held-out molecular benchmarks and potentials not used during the search. Most notably, at the r2SCAN-3c DFT level, the best variant requires only 40 _._ 2–77 _._ 2% of Sella’s force calls while achieving the same energy reduction, even though agent used no DFT gradients.

[2610.08020#16] **4 Discussion and Conclusions**
Our results demonstrate that `grappa-fullFF` is an end-to-end force field that learns bonded and nonbonded parameters directly from ab-initio QM energies and forces. One might expect this approach to introduce a degeneracy between interaction terms, but we show that this ambiguity can be resolved through physics-inspired regularization. By constraining charge-conserving bond fluxes through the electrostatic potential and LJ parameters through the TS-vdW volume ratios, our 5 model learns parameters which are physically consistent and transferable. For instance, we obtain reduced LJ _σ_ values for polar hydrogens required for hydrogen bonding, despite the larger values that would result from using TS-vdW volume ratios directly (Appendix C). These nonbonded parameters (charges, LJ parameters) emerge implicitly, without having been optimized against reference values, and offer considerably cheaper alternatives to methods such as MBIS that rely on expensive electron density calculations and partitioning. This parameter flexibility does not compromise the accuracy of bonded interactions. `grappa-fullFF` matches the state-of-the-art performance of `grappa-bonded` on geometry optimization and, despite being trained exclusively on isolated gas-phase monomers, reproduces conformational thermodynamics in explicit solvent. Extending training to explicit-solvent configurations will be a next step toward further refining model accuracy, along with additional refinement steps or alternative charge initialization schemes

However, many scientific challenges demand molecules with very rare properties, and in this sparse setting, existing algorithms offer little gain over random guessing. We propose a method to efficiently search large regions of molecular space using algorithmically controlled stochastic synthesis. Rather than design, make and test individual molecules, we design and make complex mixtures, test them as a pool, then deconvolute the molecule-activity map. [2610.08495#0] Information-Dense Synthesis for Molecular Discovery
Kasper K. Jakobsen<sup>_∗_</sup> & Eli N. Weinstein<sup>∗</sup> October 7, 2026 ##### **Abstract** Machine learning can accelerate molecular discovery by designing molecules and planning experiments. However, many scientific challenges demand molecules with very rare properties, and in this sparse setting, existing algorithms offer little gain over random guessing. We propose a method to efficiently search large regions of molecular space using algorithmically controlled stochastic synthesis. Rather than design, make and test individual molecules, we design and make complex mixtures, test them as a pool, then deconvolute the molecule-activity map. We optimize synthesis to encode maximal information. Theoretically, this approach can reduce the number of experiments required to find the optimal molecule among _d_ candidates from _O_ ( _d_ ) to _O_ (log _d_ ) or _O_ (1). In simulation, on estimated protein fitness landscapes, it finds active molecules with an order of magnitude fewer experiments than existing Bayesian optimization methods.

Given that the quantum mechanical equations that define the various levels of theory are typically solved iteratively, using information from previous geometry optimization steps to provide an accurate guess to such an iterative procedure is an attractive way to reduce the overall computational cost of the optimization. Recently, Polack et al. proposed an extrapolation method aiming to get sophisticated initial guess strategies for Hartree Fock (HF) and Density Functional Theory (DFT) in the context of Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics (BOMD) [24–27]. In a Taylor-based approach, the calculated quantities at the previous geometries are used to build an ansatz that serves as an initial guess, incorporating information about the new geometry via a so-called molecular descriptor. 1 In this contribution, we propose a conceptually similar strategy that can be applied to Coupled Cluster optimizations. amplitudes by solving a large system of nonlinear equations using an iterative quasi-Newton method [30]. The main computational bottleneck lies in the evaluation of the residual at each Newton step, with a formal _O_ ( _N_<sup>6</sup> ) computational scaling. This high computational cost restricts the application of CCSD to medium-sized systems. The calculation of CC analytical gradients is about twice as expensive as the energy calculation, since the Λ equations have the same scaling, and overall similar computational cost, as the amplitude equations. For this reason, various strategies were proposed in the literature to reduce the computational cost and memory requirements while preserving accuracy, for instance exploiting the local nature of dynamic electron correlation [31–43] or using rank-reducing techniques [44–56]. From a different, yet complementary, perspective, fewer attempts have been made to provide a better guess for solving the CC equations, thus reducing the overall number of iterations during a geometry optimization procedure. [2610.09151#0] Coupled Cluster Amplitude Extrapolation in Geometry Optimization
Jonas Beck<sup>1</sup> , Michele Nottoli<sup>1</sup> , Tommaso Nottoli<sup>2</sup> , Luca Melega<sup>2</sup> , Filippo Lipparini<sup>2</sup> , and Benjamin Stamm<sup>1</sup> > 1Institute of Applied Analysis and Numerical Simulation, University of Stuttgart, Pfaffenwaldring 57, 70569 Stuttgart, Germany > 2Dipartimento di Chimica e Chimica Industriale Via Moruzzi 13, 56124 Pisa, Italy *Email: jonas.beck@ians.uni-stuttgart.de #### **Abstract** In this work, we present an amplitude extrapolation ansatz for geometry optimization that uses calculations from previous steps to construct an initial guess for the quasi-Newton solver at each new geometry, significantly accelerating convergence of the coupled-cluster and Lambda solver alike. The ansatz incorporates a necessary amplitude transformation to mitigate discontinuities associated with orbital energy crossings at the Hartree–Fock level of theory, while remaining computational and memory efficient. The method is tested for a diverse set of medium-sized molecules to demonstrate a systematic and significant reduction in the number of coupled-cluster iterations compared to the conventional method.

Geometry optimizations have been performed using geomeTRIC [68, 69] as the main driver, which in turns uses CFOUR as the electronic structure engine [70, 71], and a custom Python module for providing initial guess amplitudes, which implements the extrapolation algorithm and the orbital transformation described in the previous section. The convergence criteria in geomeTRIC were set to _|_ ∆ _E|_ < 1.0e-06 _Eh_ , RMS-Grad < 1.0e-05 _Eh/a_ 0, Max-Grad < 4.5e-04 _Eh/a_ 0, RMSD <1.2e-03 Å and Max-Disp <1.8e-03 Å, where RMSD 6 is the root-mean-square displacement. All systems analyzed numerically are initialized with the starting nuclear geometry, obtained via a DFT geometry optimization in PySCF, with the functional _ω_ B97X-V and the def2-TZVP basis set [72–75]. The DFT level geometry optimizations have been accelerated using the DFT version of G-Ext [24–26]. For all the investigated molecules, CC calculations have been performed using the cc-pVTZ basis set[76–78].

[2610.09268#1] **I. INTRODUCTION**
Hybrid ion–atom systems combine trapped ions with ultracold atomic gases, providing a platform for investigating interactions between charged and neutral particles [1–5]. Studies of cold collisions and chemical reactions have revealed the rich dynamics arising from these interactions [6–13], while the observation of ion–atom Feshbach resonances has opened a route to controlling them [14, 15], analogous to the control achieved in ultracold neutral gases [16]. Realizing this potential requires control over the ion’s translational motion, which is governed by its interactions with both the atomic bath and the trapping field. In a radiofrequency trap, collisions can couple the driven micromotion to the ion’s secular motion, producing a nonequilibrium steady state whose energy distribution differs from that of the surrounding gas [17, 18]. Understanding this energy exchange is therefore essential for controlling collision energies and accessing the quantum regime of ion–atom interactions. The energy relaxation of a single trapped ion immersed in an atomic gas has been investigated using several complementary approaches. Within classical descriptions, these include Monte Carlo collision models [18], Langevin-type stochastic equations [19], and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations [20, 21]. Monte Carlo collision models propagate the ion in the trapping field between instantaneous collisions, whose occurrence and outcomes

[2610.09268#2] **I. INTRODUCTION**
are sampled according to prescribed collision rates and scattering laws, often based on the Langevin capture model. Langevin-type approaches instead represent the bath through friction and fluctuating forces, with the ion–atom interaction entering the associated transport coefficients. MD simulations resolve the collision by propagating the coupled motion of the ion and a single atom under their interaction potential and the trapping field. These simulations capture finite-duration encounters, collision-induced energy exchange with the trap, and the formation of transient ion–atom complexes. Despite their detailed treatment of individual encounters, commonly used MD implementations introduce atoms sequentially, allowing only one atom to interact with the ion at a time. We refer to this implementation as the “one-atom-at-a-time” approach. This approximation describes isolated binary encounters but excludes the arrival of an additional atom while a collision or transient complex is still evolving. Its validity therefore depends on the separation between the duration of an encounter and the waiting time for another atom to reach the interaction region. Long-lived ion–atom complexes can challenge this separation even in a dilute gas, allowing additional atoms to participate before the complex dissociates [22, 23]. [2610.09268#0] **Full molecular dynamics simulations of a single trapped ion in a neutral bath**
Saajid Chowdhury, Ruiren Shi, and Jes´us P´erez-R´ıos _Department of Physics and Astronomy, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY 11794, USA_ We present full molecular dynamics simulations that explicitly incorporate the simultaneous interactions between a trapped ion and a bath of neutral atoms. In contrast to conventional molecular dynamics treatments, this framework enables a systematic assessment of how the atomic-gas density influences both the ion’s cooling dynamics and its steady-state mean kinetic energy. Our results show that the gas density measurably modifies the ion’s average kinetic energy, albeit only weakly, in qualitative disagreement with predictions obtained from standard molecular dynamics simulations. In addition, the calculations indicate that short-range features of the atom–ion interaction potential become increasingly consequential as the atomic density increases. Simulations including many atoms yield higher mean kinetic energies than standard molecular dynamics, a trend we attribute to the transient formation of molecular-ion complexes. Finally, we observe that for a fixed ion, lighter atomic baths lead to a smaller final ion average kinetic energy than heavier atomic baths.

[2610.09268#1] **I. INTRODUCTION**
Hybrid ion–atom systems combine trapped ions with ultracold atomic gases, providing a platform for investigating interactions between charged and neutral particles [1–5]. Studies of cold collisions and chemical reactions have revealed the rich dynamics arising from these interactions [6–13], while the observation of ion–atom Feshbach resonances has opened a route to controlling them [14, 15], analogous to the control achieved in ultracold neutral gases [16]. Realizing this potential requires control over the ion’s translational motion, which is governed by its interactions with both the atomic bath and the trapping field. In a radiofrequency trap, collisions can couple the driven micromotion to the ion’s secular motion, producing a nonequilibrium steady state whose energy distribution differs from that of the surrounding gas [17, 18]. Understanding this energy exchange is therefore essential for controlling collision energies and accessing the quantum regime of ion–atom interactions. The energy relaxation of a single trapped ion immersed in an atomic gas has been investigated using several complementary approaches. Within classical descriptions, these include Monte Carlo collision models [18], Langevin-type stochastic equations [19], and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations [20, 21]. Monte Carlo collision models propagate the ion in the trapping field between instantaneous collisions, whose occurrence and outcomes

Langevin-type approaches instead represent the bath through friction and fluctuating forces, with the ion–atom interaction entering the associated transport coefficients. It is obtained via the Fourier transform of the velocity autocorrelation function. The VDOS can be computed separately for each component of the system, probing distinct vibrational processes across a broad frequency range. For a system with _N_ species, this yields _N_ species-resolved VDOS (here we consider O and H), computed for both the reference and each XC approximation, and evaluated in the same two environments as the RDFs, bulk water and interfacial water. Using a norm _d_VDOS analogous to that used for the RDFs, we obtain a measure of similarity between the RPA/QZ and XC VDOS spectra for each species and environment. Averaging over species and then over environments, and converting the result to a percentage, yields the overall score for a given XC approximation. _Spain_| Simulations of water at solid interfaces routinely disagree on basic properties, from contact angle to friction, depending on the model used, whether an empirical force field or a density functional theory (DFT) exchangecorrelation (XC) approximation. Yet no accurate computational reference has been available to determine which, if any, is reliable. Here we assess XC approximations spanning the rungs of Jacob’s Ladder against the random-phase approximation (RPA) at the graphene–water interface. Using machine-learned potentials (MLPs) trained on both DFT and RPA data, we achieve the extensive sampling required to characterize interfacial structure, wettability, friction, and vibrational sum-frequency generation spectra. [2610.09685#1] head We find that XC approximations disagree substantially with RPA and with each other. To make sense of this, we introduce a transferable, multi-observable scoring framework that distills each functional’s agreement with RPA into a single measure. Six functionals emerge as reliable starting points for studies of graphene–water and other dispersion-dominated interfaces, namely B3LYP-D3(0), revPBE-D3(0), revPBE-D3(BJ), B97M-rV, r2 SCAN, and revPBE0-D3(0). Notably, this ranking follows no simple rule based on functional family or rung of Jacob’s Ladder. What does hold across functionals is that dynamical and spectroscopic properties tend to be harder for DFT to reproduce than structural ones, with direct consequences for functional selection. Our framework also offers a general strategy for benchmarking any atomistic model, including the new generation of foundational MLPs, against high-accuracy references at solid–liquid interfaces. Beyond simulation, this work identifies which models can be trusted to connect measured contact angles, friction, and vibrational spectra to the molecular structure behind them. /no_think

In these simulations, we explore two limiting scenarios in which the surface charge is treated as either entirely localized or entirely delocalized, corresponding to the limiting cases of CaF2 surface charging and graphene charging in our experimental system, respectively. Asymmetries upon charge reversal are commonly attributed to specific ion adsorption or surface chemistry. Yet it is unresolved whether interfacial water is net oriented at zero charge, and whether such orientation alone makes its response charge-asymmetric. Here, using electrochemical heterodyne-detected sum-frequency generation spectroscopy and constant-potential molecular dynamics simulations, we resolve the absolute orientation of water at a weakly interacting graphene electrode. We show that interfacial water retains a net H-down orientation, with hydrogens pointing toward the bulk, at zero net surface charge. Superimposed on this offset, the field-induced reorientation is linear and symmetric upon charge reversal, independent of how the charge is introduced or distributed. The unequal response of a system to positive and negative charges of equal magnitude, usually referred to as charge asymmetry, is ubiquitous in aqueous interfacial chemistry and biology. Its manifestations are evident even at macroscopic interfaces: in electrowetting, water on hydrophobic dielectrics responds differently to positive and negative voltages [1], while supercooled water freezes at higher temperatures on positively than on negatively charged pyroelectric surfaces [2]. Beyond planar interfaces, like-charged colloids interact in a sign-dependent manner: in water, negatively charged particles attract one another at long range, whereas positively charged ones repel [3]. In biology, protein stability and solubility likewise depend asymmetrically on the sign of dissolved ions, as reflected in the distinct anionic and cationic Hofmeister series [4, 5]. Specific mechanisms have been identified in some of these cases, including trapped charge in electrowetting [6], ion partitioning in electrofreezing [7], and distinct binding sites for anions and cations on proteins [4]. Yet it remains unresolved whether, and to what extent, water itself accounts for this charge asymmetry beyond extrinsic contributions such as specific ion adsorption and surface chemistry. The success of the BSE comes from a screened Coulomb interaction that explicitly accounts for interactions between electrons and holes.[37–43] The BSE has become a benchmark approach for molecular and condensed-phase spectroscopy, but generating the screened Coulomb matrix elements scales quartically with system size. This has limited application to large-scale molecular aggregate settings.[40–49] As a result, a large gap persists between experimentally relevant molecular aggregates and the many-body methods needed to describe them. Our recent developments in stochastic many-body theory provide a route toward closing this gap.[50–57] By replacing the explicit construction of the real-space 3 screened Coulomb operator with stochastic realizations of the operator’s action, these approaches retain the essential many-body physics of the BSE while substantially reducing computational cost. [2610.10298#7] 1 INTRODUCTION
Many computational chemistry applications aim to accurately approximate the electronic ground state of molecules and materials. The rapid developments in this field are driven by the abundance of applications enabling the _in silico_ prescreening of potential materials and drugs before moving into resource- and time-intensive laboratory experiments or clinical trials. Since the exact computation of the ground state is intractable for almost all systems of interest, the art of computational chemistry is to find the correct trade-off between accuracy and computational cost for a given application (Szabo & Ostlund, 1996). Contemporary method development pushes this Pareto frontier as far as possible. For many applications, KS-DFT (Kohn & Sham, 1965) is the method of choice (Antypas et al., 2014; Haunschild et al., 2019).
